“Red One” is relatively watchable family fare, but as ephemeral and forgettable as a first dusting of snow.

An ugly, under-lit, joyless slog, devoid of any holiday charm or sense of fun.

It's worth hanging in there, because [Chris Evans and Dwayne Johnson] are just so fun to watch together. They know how to sell a big action movie.

Red One is incredibly bland.

While not as egregious as its initial trailer, this movie seemingly takes a note from every recent generic action-comedy blockbuster, stitches it together with some Christmas tropes, and hopes its recognizable cast can carry the experience.
Red One may be wrapped differently but brings the same warm festive cheer needed during the merry season. A bit of action and a lot of heart.
It’s not the gift you were hoping for but it’s also not a lump of coal.
If you want to see a decent X-Mas film, this spiritless and convoluted atrocity is not it.
Language is too rpugh for a family film so who does that leave?
It is not a classic at all.

Action-and-gadget-packed, comedic Mission Impossible-style movie for an early holiday cheer. If the child in you ever wonder how Santa can drop off gifts to billions of people around the world in one night, you'll be in for a fantastical holiday treat!

The film lacks too many elements to be a holiday classic. The first half is all over the place, but I did enjoy the mistletoe mayhem in the second act. It gets better when Krampus (played by Kristofer Hivju) shows up.
If this is what Red One is, don't expect a Red Two.
Red One film thinks it's much more clever than it is. Evans is doing his best Ryan Reynolds impression combined with Johnson's self seriousness makes for a ho ho ho-hum time at the movies.

This holiday film plays it safe and lands somewhere in that weird middle ground where it can’t decide whether it wants to be edgy or family-friendly. The result is a head-scratching exercise in total confusion and missed potential.
This is the big American blockbuster of the week, and it is absolute crap.

“Red One,” a film that has the courage to ask: What if the Santa Claus story was like a Marvel movie?

Momentary world-building fades away quickly in this chemistry-free effort that takes itself way too seriously and is indistinguishable from the lavishly expensive but creative dead zones too often associated with films that go-to-streaming for a reason.
It’s wildly overproduced blockbuster silliness, but with some genuine witty imagination.

JK Simmons raises an occasional smile as a keep-fit enthusiast Santa, and Kiernan Shipka has fun as a witchy foe, but they're rare bright spots in an otherwise formulaic yarn that brings very little in the way of glad tidings.
Lower your bar, and you’ll be delightfully entertained.
RED ONE is bold to include hard hits, tough language and a seriously relevant theme in a Christmas film.
But what “Red One” is really missing, what every Christmas movie worth its eggnog requires, is summed up in one word: magic.
While Red One boasts an impressive cast and a festive backdrop, it struggles to deliver the magic and heart of a true Christmas classic.

Serviceable for those seeking a Christmas-based adventure. It just lacks the kind of personality that would make it memorable.

Such a noisy, witless puddle of CGI puke I can’t believe Ryan Reynolds isn’t in it.

... darker than advertised and somewhat monstrous... more ambitious than it will be credited for, the film takes big swings and only asks audiences to enjoy the ride, happily imperfect and overstuffed.

Loud, stupid, and filled with ugly CGI.

Makes the worst sin of all. It's boring. I couldn't wait for it to be over

I really enjoyed Red One, not only for its modern take on a tired trope but also for its dovetailing of other Yuletide myths into a decidedly Western monopoly. It’s warm and funnyn with familiarity that is profoundly amusing.

Bombastic and obnoxious—but with a sickeningly sweet dose of sentiment at the end—this charmless, CGI-heavy behemoth is enough to make you dread the coming season.
Red One is bonkers enough to make you giggle, giving you a break from the usual holiday flick, if you don’t mind a Christmas movie with a side of overly elaborate big-budget superhero-style action.
Red One begins with a bland conceit. The movie's reliance on formula and hesitation to flex any imaginative muscle, though, makes it tedious.

A Yuletide misfire that lands like a lump of coal.
Same old, same old from The Rock at this point. Nothing you haven't seen before.
This grossly overstuffed Christmas stocking of charmless Yule-adjacent mayhem is a big ho-ho-ho no thanks.

Solid ideas twisting mythology is a decent starting point, but relying on excessive hideous CGI, laughably asinine self-serious tone, and charisma-zapped Evans and Johnson duo, this is as disastrous as a flying sled crashing into some poor bastard’s home
It's fun and offers a fresh take on a Christmas tale. Loved the world-building around the mythical world and the banter between Dwayne Johnson and Chris Evans.

Despite all the mythical creatures and goofy, comedic special effects, “Red One” is less fun than it should be. Any warm and fuzzy feelings generated by the film are immediately interrupted by an action sequence.
We can all use a reaffirming message this holiday season, but this stuffs stockings with little more than hot air. I’d have preferred some coal. There’s at least a use for that.

The most charming thing about the movie, Santa Clause, is only in it for about 10 minutes. It's just so thin and clumsy on story.  And there's no warm and creamy holiday center like a lot of the classics. What a waste.
Yuletide romp offers bromance, some laughs and way too much plot.
The Rock is back with Red One, a film so relentlessly lackluster and uninspired that I wondered if it was a cruel holiday prank meant to ruin our Christmas spirit.

Santa Claus militarized as Tom Clancy would have imagined him, Red One is a non-stop action movie with just enough plot to stitch together more action scenes, as soullessly fast and furious as you’d expect from writer Chris Morgan of Fast & Furious fame.
The Red One haters are just naughty-listers. It’s a fun and creative take on the holiday spirit.
Red One is not the lump of coal in your stocking that you thought it’d be. That doesn’t mean it's a pretty present under your tree either.
Will probably be forgotten before December even arrives.

There's a scene early on where Dwayne Johnson is helping a jacked Santa Claus work out in the North Pole gym, and is spotting him while talking about how he might be losing the spirit of Christmas, where I thought to myself "What are we doing here?"
While the yuletide sentiments are thin as store brand egg nog, cool visuals, clever twists on Christmas mythology, and a fully committed ensemble make for a gift worth unwrapping.
It’s an absolute blast of a Christmas flick that doesn’t take itself too seriously.

A mixed bag but I actually think families & young kids will enjoy this. If a Christmas movie can nail down the holiday spirit then it’s something to add to my Christmas movie rotation & Red One has earned a spot even if it wont be for all.
The picture may be unoriginal at times and downright silly at others, but the Christmas cheer at its heart is rewardingly uncomplicated.

Everything that is “wrong” about Red One could have been fixed by 2 simple principles. Pace it up and tone it down for families. It should have been riding the edge of a G rating instead of pushing the edge of the R. They didn’t need it.
There's not much that's holly or jolly about this salty Christmas monster mash, but tweens and teens may be just fine with an entertaining action movie about Santa.

The Christmas action comedy Red One is the equivalent of Santa Claus delivering an avalanche of coal. The incoherent plot is about rescuing a kidnapped Santa, but viewers will feel like the ones being taken hostage by this unfunny and bloated abomination.
[Red One] is a little self-aware about its own inherent silliness. But not nearly enough. There is a better, funnier movie underneath all the CGI gloss.
What sets this apart is the odd couple pairing of Dwayne Johnson and Chris Evans. Even if it's undercooked, their banter provides entertaining festive cheer.

Red One is weakly written and unevenly directed: effects-heavy action sequences alternate with lifeless interludes of Christmas-themed banter, edited in a manner that suggests the stars spent only a limited amount of time together on set.
High-tech and low-charm, this is the sort of film you make to fund an extension, or buy a fleet of unwanted drones for your whole family.
“Red One” is deadening to watch, as so much technical and thespian effort has gone into a feature that carries no sense of spirit.

…two hours plus of CGI slop, which plays like 1985’s Santa Claus the Movie reimagined as a stale heist movie with goblins… a garish, ghastly movie that will bore kids and depress adults...

Gross, grim yuletide yuck.

Red One is an action-packed holiday showdown. [...] They level up the holiday magic we know and love, while adding a fresh perspective with mythological characters we don’t often see represented. A blast for the whole family!
Given the amount of Christmas classics re-released in the lead up to the big day, there’s little reason to get roped into this lifeless caper.
It’s an odd film that doesn’t seem to know what it wants for Christmas.

The irony is apparently lost on the filmmakers that this movie is literally a product of Amazon... which only partially explains why it feels like the kind of soulless, cynical item that one orders close to Christmas without any thought or effort.

It's a film so bereft of genuine emotion that I can't imagine even the most desperate Christmas fans getting anything out of it. Why bother scaring kids with lumps of coal when the alternative is to make them sit through this mess?

Painfully unfunny, witless, over-produced and tonally uneven mess with an uninspired and convoluted plot that's too silly for adults and too dull for kids. It's one of the worst Christmas movies since Jingle All the Way.

[A] buddy cop caper that delivers magic and laughter that doesn’t solely depend on yuletide greetings to entertain.

Red One isn't a cinematic masterpiece and suffers from Johnson's predictable performance. However, thanks to Evans' charm, the film delivers on its promise of entertaining escapism with plenty of action and holiday cheer.
Big name stars collide for a festive adventure that's big on effects and spectacle but curiously lacks any of the charm of the holidays.
Jake Kasdan’s action comedy [is] apparently geared towards prepubescent boys who think Christmas does not have enough firepower – or trolls, witches, torture chambers, slap fights and car chases.

There's a little bit of heart here, in the story of two people who have lost faith in Christmas for very different reasons, but more often this feels engineered in a lab to provide seasonal spectacle.

Red One offers a surprisingly clever take on Christmas mythology. The big-budget action-comedy delivers the requisite popcorn entertainment with visual splendor, but also succeeds in building its own new universe with memorable characters.
Not every film has to be art, but it’d be nice if they could make product that had more life to it than this empty exercise in Christmas franchise starting.

Considering the huge lump of comedic coal this could have been, I’ll gladly take a decent present that entertains me for a few hours.

This is what I have wanted for a long time. An intelligent action movie that remembers that characterisation is important. The exploration of mythology is a nice touch - this just became one of my go to annual Christmas films.
You're left with an overwhelming confusion over who Red One is actually aimed at.
For a movie centred around the festive season and attempts to drive home the importance of joy, there’s very little on offer when it comes to the unnecessarily long 122 minutes of Red One.

The challenge is to balance the mayhem with the holly-jolly, to blow stuff up while also allowing troubled characters to find the nice in themselves and in each other, and Red One fulfills both of those wish-list items with a cheeky finesse.
It’s like when a toddler hands you a fake phone, you answer that call. Kasdan and screenwriter Chris Morgan definitely answered the call.
Possibly one of the most misguided holiday movies ever made. Instead of putting you into the Xmas spirit, it makes you feel as if you’ve just been force-fed a giant lump of coal.

This film would have worked if it leaned more into the humor, but it doesn’t muster up more than the occasional chuckle, mainly with Evans responding to the insanity surrounding him. Beyond that, Red One won’t be the Christmas classic it hopes to be.

It is a movie that is playing in front of you, I can comfortably give it that much, and for one meant to summon up the Christmas spirit, there’s not a whiff of mirth from the screenplay to the production level.
It all averages out to slightly above average. For a film like 'Red One' that’s about as good as anyone could hope for.
The mixture of laughs, sentiment and action should satisfy undemanding families, and the story’s world-building offers enough novelty to what can otherwise be a predictable package.
If Red One were a disaster, it’d be more interesting. Instead, it’s a technically passable action-comedy transparently stitched together from parts scavenged from other movies.

A high-concept genre hybrid of a Christmas movie that belongs on the naughty list.
This is a high-concept, CG-saturated bore that lacks heart and infectious humor, even if it huffs and puffs its way to a little poignancy in the end.
There’s nothing wrong with a big-hearted film for Christmas, but this commercial and formulaic slice of content is a toy destined to be forgotten, not by Boxing Day, but mid-November.
